Upon her arrival at Bucharest’s airport, President Murmu was warmly welcomed by Romania’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Oana-Silvia Țoiu , in a gesture reflecting the importance both nations attach to their bilateral partnership. Upon her arrival at Bucharest’s airport, President Murmu was warmly welcomed by Romania’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Oana-Silvia Țoiu, in a gesture reflecting the importance both nations attach to their bilateral partnership. The visit is expected to provide fresh momentum to India-Romania relations, which have steadily expanded over the years across political dialogue, trade, investment, education, culture, information technology, and people-to-people exchanges. Romania and India have enjoyed diplomatic relations for more than seven decades, with both countries sharing a commitment to democratic values, international cooperation, and regional stability. Against the backdrop of evolving geopolitical and economic realities, the State Visit offers an opportunity to further deepen cooperation in areas of mutual strategic interest, including economic development, innovation, digital transformation, energy security, defense, and connectivity. President Murmu’s visit is also expected to reaffirm the growing engagement between India and Central and Eastern Europe, while highlighting Romania’s role as an important partner for New Delhi within the European Union and the Black Sea region. The visit marks another milestone in the strengthening of the multifaceted partnership between India and Romania, underscoring the shared determination of both governments to expand cooperation and build on decades of friendly relations. According to the Embassy of India in Romania, President Murmu’s State Visit represents “an important milestone in further strengthening the longstanding and multifaceted partnership between India and Romania.” The visit is expected to include high-level meetings with Romanian officials and discussions aimed at enhancing bilateral cooperation across a broad range of sectors, reaffirming the commitment of both countries to elevating their strategic dialogue and deepening their partnership in the years ahead. 23.07.2026 Explore our Digital Edition archives available in more than 150 countries (2024–2025–2026) Nine O’Clock Daily (Romania) Online Archive | Back Issues 2024 – 2025 – 2026 Nine O’Clock Weekly (Romania) Online Archive | Back Issues 2024 – 2025 -2026 Nine O’Clock Yearbook (Romania) Online Archive | Back Issues 2024 – 2025 Social media Nine O`Clock: Pagina LinkedIn https://www.linkedin.com/company/nineoclock Pagina Facebook https://www.facebook.com/nineoclockromania/ Pagina Instagram https://www.instagram.com/nineoclockro/ Pagina Twitter https://twitter.com/Nine O’Clock The diplomatic daily newspaper Nine O’Clock does not assume responsibility for the information received and published on the public website. https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/in.text: Ukraine War Escalates as Black Sea Drone Strikes Hit Cargo Ships October 6, 2026 by Slav Okov Attacks on commercial vessels off the Black Sea’s western coast are on the rise, threatening already-choked trade flows in the region while testing NATO’s readiness to react. Two general cargo ships were hit by air and naval drones overnight in the exclusive economic zone of Bulgaria, a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters on Tuesday. A commercial vessel loaded with rapeseed oil was also damaged by a Russian drone strike that killed one person on Tuesday, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper said on Telegram. The overnight strikes are “absolutely unacceptable” and in violation of international law and maritime practice, Radev told reporters, without naming the source of the attack. “What is happening severely hampers shipping in the Black Sea, drives up insurance costs even further, and makes maritime operations extremely difficult.” The strikes in NATO countries’ exclusive economic zones add to previous cases of drone incursions in countries such as Poland and Romania, helping Russia to test the alliance’s readiness to protect its borders while remaining short of full-fledged attacks on its territory. They also reflect how the Black Sea is becoming an increasingly precarious corridor for agricultural trade, raising concerns over how crops from two of the world’s biggest exporters — Russia and Ukraine — will reach global buyers. Ports along the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts, including Constanta, Varna and Burgas, have provided important alternatives for traders navigating disruptions elsewhere in the region. Growing risks around those routes threaten to narrow those options further, with potential consequences for freight costs and grain prices. Radev said the strikes can’t trigger NATO’s protective clauses — including formal consultations and the principle that an attack against one member state is an attack against the alliance — on the ground that more serious incidents have happened in the past without such a forceful response. He said it’s up to NATO’s leadership to to consider the nature and form of that response. “Ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea, and there are frequent drone strikes against vessels,” he said at an event in Sofia later on Tuesday, warning that long conflicts tend to expand geographically. A cargo vessel also caught fire and sank Monday in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, with two crew members found dead. The ship that carried corn was Turkish-owned and hit by two Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. A passing Bulgarian ferry saved the 18 crew members of the ship sailing under the flag of Palau that caught fire, which Radev said was carrying wheat. The other ship struck in the overnight attack sank with no information on its crew or its cargo. A search and rescue operation for the crew of the Togolese-flagged vessel is ongoing. “Freedom of navigation becomes meaningless if Russia can make exercising it a matter of risking a civilian crew and vessel,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X on Tuesday. “Russia should not be allowed to impose this hidden tax on international trade through violence and insecurity,” he said. The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning. Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea. Today, two commercial vessels were hit in Bulgaria’s economic zone in Black Sea. This comes just one day after a Turkish ship… — Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 6, 2026 Bulgarian authorities are monitoring another ship drifting off the Bulgarian coast, hit in August and without crew, he said. Authorities may take action if it reaches territorial waters. President Iliana Yotova called a security council meeting to discuss on Wednesday the risks from Russia’s ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Madeleine Overgaard, senior manager for agriculture data at Kpler, said that both vessels hit in the overnight attack were sailing to or from Ukrainian ports. There’s no clear evidence of a direct threat to ships using the major Bulgarian and Romanian ports, she said. “Still, the attacks widen the high-risk area. Ships may now face greater risks as soon as they enter the Black Sea, rather than only when approaching Ukrainian ports,” Overgaard said.
